summary: This experimental RFC extends PCEP so a central path computation element can control paths in native IP networks, an approach called Centralized Control Dynamic Routing (CCDR). A PCE can then calculate and manage routing paths in networks that do not use MPLS or similar tunnels.

eli5.summary: Usually every road sign decides for itself. Here one traffic controller plans the routes and tells ordinary IP routers which way to send traffic.

questions: how does pcep control native ip networks
subtitle: Central control of paths in plain IP networks without MPLS tunneling

tldr.problem: Traffic engineering in traditional IP networks is difficult because routers make independent routing decisions. Most traffic engineering uses MPLS, but not all networks deploy MPLS. There is no standard way for a central controller to manage paths in native IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends PCEP (the protocol used to talk to path computation elements) so a central controller can instruct routers to establish BGP sessions with each other and advertise specific prefixes over those sessions, creating controlled paths without MPLS tunnels.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now do traffic engineering and path control using only IP and BGP, with a central PCE coordinating the paths. This is useful for networks that want to avoid the complexity of MPLS but still need to control traffic.

facts.label: New Objects
facts.value: BPI (BGP Peer Info), EPR (Explicit Peer Route), PPA (Peer Prefix Advertisement)

facts.label: Forwarding modes
facts.value: Raw mode (destination-based) and Tunnel mode (entry-exit specific)

today: RFC 9757 is an Experimental specification designed to test whether PCE-based central control of native IP networks is practical. The RFC encourages implementation and deployment to gather feedback on scalability and operational impact before considering advancement to the Standards Track.

sections.title: Central Control for IP Networks
sections.content:
PCEP is the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol, normally used to ask a central server (the PCE) to compute the best path for MPLS tunnels. But in native IP networks—networks that do not use MPLS—each router simply forwards based on the destination address and BGP routing, with no way for a central controller to manage paths.

This RFC extends PCEP to let a PCE control routing in native IP networks by orchestrating BGP sessions. The PCE tells routers which BGP peers to establish sessions with, what prefixes to advertise over those sessions, and what explicit routes to use. By controlling the BGP advertisements and routing, the PCE can direct traffic through specific paths without MPLS.
sections.eli5: A central controller tells routers who they should be friends with (peers) and which addresses to talk about to those friends. By controlling the conversation, the controller directs traffic.

sections.title: BGP Session Management
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new PCEP capability and several new objects for native IP traffic engineering. When the PCE and a router (called the PCC, Path Computation Client) connect, they advertise support for native IP TE by including a Native IP flag in the capability exchange.

The PCE uses a BGP Peer Info (BPI) object to instruct a PCC to establish a BGP session with another router. The BPI contains the peer's AS number, the peer's IP address, and the local IP address to use for the BGP session. The router reports back via PCEP whether the BGP session is up, down, or still establishing, and if there are errors (e.g., the peer address is unreachable).

The PCC treats these BGP sessions as special: the Local and Peer IP addresses are dedicated to the PCEP-controlled peering and cannot be used for other BGP sessions. The PCE coordinates which routers become peers, building a network topology under central control.
sections.eli5: The controller sends a message saying: Router A, talk to Router B at this address. Router A tries, and tells the controller: OK, we are connected, or We cannot reach that address.

sections.title: Explicit Routes and Prefix Advertisement
sections.content:
Once BGP sessions are established, the PCE uses two more objects to control traffic flow:

Explicit Peer Route (EPR) object: installed on routers along the desired path, an EPR tells a router to forward packets destined for a peer address through a specific next hop. These routes have higher priority than dynamic IGP routes but lower priority than manually configured static routes. The PCE installs EPRs in reverse order (from destination toward source) to avoid forwarding loops during installation.

Peer Prefix Advertisement (PPA) object: the PCE tells a router to advertise specific prefixes to a particular BGP peer. Only the designated peer receives these prefixes; other BGP peers do not. This allows the PCE to selectively advertise destinations and force traffic through the paths it has set up.

By combining BPI (peer setup), EPR (routing), and PPA (prefix advertisement), the PCE orchestrates end-to-end paths. For example, to create a path from Router A to Router C through Router B, the PCE establishes BGP sessions A↔B and B↔C, installs routes at each hop, and advertises prefixes to push traffic along the path.
sections.eli5: The controller tells Router A: forward packets for Router C through Router B. It tells Router B: forward packets for Router C directly to Router C. And it tells Routers A and B which addresses to advertise on the BGP connection between them.

sections.title: Raw Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
The RFC offers two ways to forward traffic. Raw mode (the default) forwards traffic based on destination address only: any traffic entering the network destined for a certain address uses the controlled path to that destination, even if the traffic entered from an unexpected ingress point.

Tunnel mode provides stricter control: the ingress router encapsulates traffic in IP-in-IP tunnels (or a similar encapsulation), creating an explicit tunnel to the egress router. This ensures that traffic from a specific entry point to a specific exit point uses the controlled path. Tunnel mode is selected by setting the T (Tunnel) bit in the BPI object.

Raw mode is simpler and uses less bandwidth (no extra header), but tunnel mode offers finer-grained control and is useful when the operator wants to ensure that only specific (entry, exit) pairs follow a particular path.
sections.eli5: Raw mode: all traffic to this address goes through my path, no matter where it came from. Tunnel mode: only traffic that started at Router A goes through my path to Router C—traffic from other sources to Router C might use a different path.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main phases: setup (establishing BGP sessions with BPI), route installation (installing explicit routes with EPR), and prefix distribution (advertising prefixes with PPA). The PCE must perform these in the right order to avoid loops: EPRs are installed in reverse path order (from destination toward source), ensuring that when each router is configured, the next-hop address is reachable.

The PCC reports the status of each operation back to the PCE via PCEP report messages. If an operation fails (e.g., a peer cannot be reached, or the next-hop address is not reachable), the PCC sends an error with details, allowing the PCE to take corrective action.

Error handling is specified for common problems: mismatched AS numbers, unreachable peer addresses, address family mismatches (trying to advertise IPv4 over an IPv6 BGP session), and mismatches between the BPI and EPR peer addresses. The RFC also defines how the PCE should clean up state when paths are removed: it sends removal instructions for PPAs, EPRs, and BPIs in the correct order to avoid disrupting traffic.
sections.eli5: The controller carefully sets up the path in steps: first establish the BGP connections, then install the routes, then advertise the addresses. Each step reports success or failure. If something breaks, the controller tells the routers how to clean up.
